name: Chaga
habitat: Almost exclusively on living birch in cold northern forest. It is a long-lived infection of the tree, not a fruiting body on a dead one.
identify: A black, cracked, charcoal-like mass bursting out of a birch trunk — it looks far more like burnt wood or a canker than like a mushroom.
THE TEST: break it open. The inside is a bright rusty orange-brown, granular and corky. Black outside, rust orange inside is the pairing nothing else offers.
On LIVING birch, usually well up the trunk, often at an old wound.
Hard and dense; it has to be chopped or levered out.

lookalikes.name: Burl or canker
lookalikes.danger: Low — you have hacked at a lump of wood for nothing.
lookalikes.tell: A burl is WOOD: bark-covered, and pale wood-grained inside. Chaga is black and crumbling outside and rust-orange and granular inside, with no grain.

lookalikes.name: Black knot
lookalikes.danger: Low, but it is a different fungus entirely and has none of the tradition.
lookalikes.tell: Black knot grows on CHERRY and plum, not birch, and forms an elongated swelling wrapped around a twig rather than a bursting mass on a trunk.

lookalikes.name: Fire scar / old burn
lookalikes.tell: Charred bark is thin and flakes off to reveal wood underneath. Chaga is a deep mass with orange flesh several centimetres in.

preparations.method: Break into chunks and simmer LONG — an hour or more, never a hard boil — until the water runs dark red-brown. The same chunks re-brew several times.
preparations.for_use: A dark, mild, coffee-ish drink; traditionally taken for gut complaints and as a general tonic across northern Europe and Siberia. A brief steep extracts almost nothing — this one genuinely needs the long simmer.

preparations.method: A dry lump takes a coal and smoulders for hours without flaming.
preparations.for_use: Carrying fire — see `fire-bank-and-carry`. This is the use with the least ambiguity attached to it.

preparations.method: The orange interior, dried and shredded, takes a spark.

preparations.for_use: An astringent rinse for skin and mouth.

cautions: Chaga is high in OXALATES. Sustained heavy use has been linked to oxalate nephropathy and kidney failure, including at least one well-documented case. Do not drink it daily for months.
It has anticoagulant activity and can lower blood sugar — a real problem alongside blood thinners, diabetes medication, or surgery.
The health claims made for it commercially run far ahead of the evidence. It is a pleasant drink and a superb ember bed; treat the rest as unproven.
It grows slowly over years and harvesting kills the patch — take part of a mass and leave the base, and never take it all.
Take only from living birch. A mass on a dead or fallen tree has usually degraded.
evidence: Long traditional use in Siberia and northern Europe as a tea; substantial laboratory interest and very little clinical evidence in humans. The oxalate kidney risk, by contrast, is documented in case reports — which is why the caution is more concrete than the benefit.
